description: A team for those who are interested in health, body signals, software engineering detection and prediction. We are looking for people with basic skills in data analysis, machine learning or health to discuss and work
summary:
Long-duration space missions expose astronauts to extreme environmental and physiological challenges, including space radiation, prolonged isolation and confinement, microgravity, and other hazards associated with living in a closed space environment.
These conditions can significantly affect astronauts' health, potentially leading to immune system dysfunction, bone density loss, cardiovascular complications, and behavioral and psychological health issues.
During extended missions, astronauts must take an active role in monitoring their own health, identifying early warning signs, and making informed decisions about their well-being, often with limited access to immediate medical assistance.
Our challenge is to develop an intelligent, reliable, and user-friendly health monitoring solution that enables astronauts to collect, track, and assess key health indicators, identify potential health risks, and receive actionable insights to support timely health-related decisions throughout their missions.
details:
Astrohealth is a web app that lets an astronaut assess their own health during a long-duration mission, using the instruments already on board. It has two modules.

The physical module tracks twelve indicators, from bone density and muscle strength loss to heart rate, blood pressure, SpO₂, daily and cumulative radiation dose, intraocular pressure, body temperature, urine specific gravity, cabin CO₂ and fasting glucose. Each value is compared with nominal (green) and alert (red) thresholds from NASA’s Human Research Program and the Canadian Space Agency, and linked to a spaceflight risk such as SANS, kidney stones, hypercapnia or “Space Fever”. The astronaut explores an interactive 3D body: touching a zone shows its indicators, current status, history and associated risk. Trend charts show the measurements, a personal baseline and a 7-day forecast with a confidence range.

The mental module collects eight parameters: stress, happiness, mood, sleep quality, perceived workload, time perception, diet quality and time spent communicating with Earth. Sleep quality is not typed in: it is computed from five sleep inputs (hours slept, bedtime, time to fall asleep, night awakenings, energy on waking). The data goes to a FastAPI service with Pydantic validation, which runs a Random Forest Regressor trained on a psychometric dataset. It returns a vulnerability assessment, an alert status and recommendations.

A prediction only runs when every parameter of the page is filled in, with no exception.

What benefits does it have?

  • Early detection. It flags slow drifts (bone loss, rising radiation dose, sleep decline) before they become emergencies.
  • Autonomy. The astronaut gets an immediate interpretation without waiting for ground support.
  • A unified view. Physical and mental health sit in one tool, so a mental dip can be read next to sleep, workload and cabin conditions.
  • Clarity. Color-coded statuses, plain-language risks and a touchable body make the data easy to read under mission fatigue.
  • Reliability. Refusing to predict from incomplete data avoids misleading results.

What is the intended impact of the project?

To protect crew safety and performance on missions where help is far away. Early detection of medical and psychological risks supports vigilance during critical operations and prepares future long-duration missions. It also gives research teams a structured, threshold-based record of how conditions like isolation, confinement, radiation and cabin atmosphere affect a crew over time. On Earth, the same approach could help in isolated or high-stress environments.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Front end: React and TypeScript, with a 3D interactive body built in three.js (React Three Fiber). The human model was prepared in Blender and exported as glTF/GLB.
  • Back end: Python with FastAPI and Pydantic, serving the machine-learning models (Random Forest Regressor for mental health).
  • Data: the 12 indicators and their thresholds come from NASA HRP and CSA references. The demo uses synthetic data for a fictional astronaut on a mission of about 60 days.
  • Hardware: no custom hardware. The app runs in a web browser, on desktop and mobile. The data sources are the on-board instruments cited in the references: Bio-Monitor Smart Shirt, pulse oximeter, handgrip dynamometer, iCare tonometer, Rad-Silk dosimeter, CANS neutron spectrometer, refractometer, ECLSS sensors and glucometer/CGM. In this prototype the astronaut enters their values manually.
  • AI-assisted development: we used Claude and a coding agent for prompts, code and review. Disclose this if the challenge requires it.

How is your project creative?

  • Touchable body. A 3D body that you rotate and tap, which turns NASA’s twelve indicators into something spatial and intuitive, instead of a table of numbers.
  • One metric reused. The sleep score computed from raw sleep inputs feeds the mental-health model, so there is a single source of truth and no double entry.
  • Honest predictions. Forecasts include a confidence range and a personal baseline, and the app never shows a prediction when data is missing.
  • Space-themed design. A calm 2D identity with a small chibi astronaut on a rocket, golden stars and transparent line drawings [keep only if implemented: brain “constellations” on the mental page, and body-part animations on the body page].

What factors did your team consider?

  • Scientific grounding. Every threshold and risk is tied to NASA HRP and CSA sources.
  • Safety and honesty. The tool is educational, not a diagnosis, which the footer says. We never fabricate values or simulate predictions, and incomplete data blocks the prediction.
  • Data quality. Strict validation of types, units and ranges (Pydantic, ranges checked in the app) to avoid garbage in, garbage out.
  • Astronaut context. Low cognitive load, sober interface, motion reduced for users who need it, and an interface that works on small screens.
  • Privacy. The prototype has no accounts or personal identification.
  • Limits. Models trained on available datasets, synthetic demo data, and manual entry instead of live sensor streams. Planned next steps are direct sensor integration, offline operation and validation with real mission data.
